An iterator is an object standing at one position in a sequence: it reads the element there with
, and is compared with another iterator of the same type using
names one past the last, and a range-for loop, or any function in
, walks from one to the other without knowing anything about how the container stores its elements.

The problem is that without this common shape, an algorithm has to be rewritten once per container: one loop for something indexed by a whole number, another for something reached only by following a link from one node to the next, and a caller who wants to walk either has to know which.

The mechanism is a small hierarchy of promises, from weakest to strongest. An input iterator can be read once and moved forward. A forward iterator can also be copied and walked again from a saved position. A bidirectional iterator can move back with
. A random-access iterator can jump by any offset in one step.
only asks for an input iterator;
asks for random access, and refuses anything weaker at compile time. Writing a container's own iterator means providing
overloads, returning something meeting whichever of these an algorithm you call needs.
What it costs is the boilerplate: the member types the standard library's traits look for, both a
form, and every comparison and increment operator written by hand. Wrapping a
you already hold, and handing back its own iterator, is smaller and safer than writing a new type, and is the right choice whenever your storage already has one.

You meet this in any collection of your own that has to work in a range-for loop or feed a standard algorithm, and the interview question is exactly that: given a tiny collection, write the two functions that make it a sequence.
